checkpoints: A bare basic.publish is fire-and-forget — the producer publishes and moves on with no signal that the broker actually wrote the message to disk.
If the broker crashes between the publish and finishing the persist, the message vanishes silently and the producer has no way to know.
AMQP transactions (tx.select/tx.commit) restore the guarantee: tx.select opens a transaction and tx.commit confirms the whole batch of publishes all-or-nothing.
tx.commit is synchronous — each commit must round-trip and wait for the broker's confirmation before publishing again, so throughput collapses at scale.
Publisher confirms solve this: enabling confirm.select gives every published message its own later ack/nack asynchronously, without blocking the producer.
Confirms provide the same durable-write guarantee as transactions but much faster, which is why confirms are almost always preferred in practice over transactions.

A confirm only means something if the exchange and queue are declared durable and the message is published with the persistent flag — otherwise it just confirms storage into something that disappears on a broker restart.
To survive losing an entire node (not just a restart), the queue must also be a quorum queue, replicated via Raft and acknowledged once a majority of replicas have written.
Edge token bucket protects the API from abusive volume by rejecting excess requests upfront with 429.
A legitimate burst that gets through the edge can still translate into heavy work against a database or third-party quota — something the edge layer never touches.
The worker limiter exists exactly for that: throttling the downstream processing rate.
Together the two layers decouple how fast you ACCEPT work from how fast you PROCESS it.
That decoupling lets the system absorb a burst yet drain it at a safe rate (e.g. 10 jobs/second via BullMQ).
Because the worker limiter is enforced in shared Redis, adding more workers doesn't raise the downstream rate — exactly what's needed when guarding a fixed downstream capacity.

Dropping the worker layer misreads the problem: the edge answers 'should this request proceed at all,' while the worker answers a different question — 'what rate can downstream actually sustain' — and the two questions cannot be collapsed into one.
RabbitMQ only removes a message from a queue once the consumer acknowledges it; until then the message stays in an "unacked" state and the broker can redeliver it if the consumer connection drops.

In the given consumer, `channel.ack(msg)` runs immediately on delivery, before `await fulfillmentService.fulfill(order)` has even started — so the broker marks the message done and deletes it before any real processing has happened.

Because the ack already fired, a thrown error inside `fulfill` or a process crash (OOM, deploy restart) that happens while `fulfill` is still running leaves no unacked copy of the message anywhere, so the order is permanently lost with no chance of redelivery.

This is exactly how RabbitMQ's at-least-once delivery guarantee gets silently downgraded to at-most-once: the guarantee only holds as long as a message is deleted strictly after processing succeeds, never before.
The fix is to move `channel.ack(msg)` to after `fulfillmentService.fulfill(order)` resolves successfully, wrapping the call in a try/catch so the ack only fires on the success path.

On failure, the consumer should call `channel.nack(msg, false, false)` to send the message to a dead-letter exchange, or nack with `requeue: true` for transient failures worth retrying, instead of acking a message that was never actually processed.

Correct behavior can be verified by deliberately throwing inside `fulfill` (or killing the worker) before the ack executes and confirming the message is redelivered to another consumer, or lands in the dead-letter queue, rather than disappearing.

The bug is a data-loss correctness issue, not a style nit, and its severity scales with `prefetch`: a higher prefetch count means more messages can be sitting acked-and-considered-done in memory when the worker crashes, widening the blast radius of lost orders.
A BullMQ `worker.on("failed", ...)` listener fires once for every failed attempt of a job, not only on the final one, so it can run several times across a single job's retry lifecycle.

Pushing to the dead-letter queue unconditionally inside that listener — without comparing `job.attemptsMade` to the job's configured max attempts — dead-letters the job after its very first failure, while BullMQ's own backoff-driven retry is still running independently in the background.

A job configured with `attempts: 3` that fails once and later succeeds still leaves a stale DLQ entry for a failure that ultimately resolved fine, and a job that fails all three times produces three duplicate DLQ entries for what is really one underlying failure.

The fix is to gate the push behind `if (job.attemptsMade >= max)` where `max = job.opts.attempts ?? 1`, so a job only reaches the DLQ once its retries are truly exhausted; before that point the queue is already handling the retry on its own and the listener has nothing useful to do.

A dead-letter queue exists to isolate permanent, poison failures from healthy jobs so they don't clog the queue; dead-lettering a job on its first transient failure defeats that purpose by mixing recoverable blips in with genuinely broken jobs.

If anything downstream consumes the DLQ — an alert, a replay job, a charge — each premature or duplicate entry re-triggers that consumer, so a side effect tied to the job that isn't idempotent can fire more than once for the same underlying failure.

Correct behavior can be verified with two cases: a job that fails a couple of times and then succeeds should never produce a DLQ entry, and a job that fails on every attempt should produce exactly one DLQ entry, added only after the final configured attempt is spent.

Splitting a rate limiter into a separate `redis.get` to read the count and a later `redis.set` to write it back creates a check-then-decrement gap: nothing prevents another request from reading the same stale count in between the two round-trips.

When two concurrent requests both read `remaining === 1` before either one writes, both pass the `remaining <= 0` check and both set the key to `0` — one request that should have been rejected gets through, and the limit is silently exceeded.
A test suite that issues requests sequentially can never expose this bug, because there is no interleaving between separate single-threaded calls — the race only appears under real concurrency.

The underlying fix is to make the whole read-compare-decrement-write sequence a single indivisible operation instead of three separate calls to Redis with the event loop free to interleave other requests in between.

Loading a Lua script once via `redis.script("LOAD", ...)` and invoking it with `redis.evalsha(sha, 1, key, ...)` moves the entire read-decide-write logic onto Redis, which executes Lua scripts single-threaded and atomically, so no other request can slip in between the read and the write.

Storing the counter in a per-instance in-memory map is a second, independent bug: each pod counts requests on its own, so N replicas behind a load balancer let a client through at N times the intended limit — the counter needs to live in one shared Redis key, not per-instance memory.
A non-atomic rate limiter is a correctness blocker, not a nitpick, and should be called out as such and kept separate from smaller nitpicks like a hardcoded TTL that could be a named constant.

Verifying an atomicity fix requires a concurrency test that fires many requests in parallel for the same key and asserts exactly the configured capacity of them succeed, since a sequential test structurally cannot exercise the interleaving window.
A sorted set is a skip list that Redis keeps sorted by score.
ZADD inserts/updates a member with O(log N) complexity.
ZREVRANGE key 0 N-1 reads the top-N already sorted directly from the skip list, with no re-scan or re-sort running on every call.
Only the N requested elements cross the network — not the whole dataset.
A sorted set also gives a member's rank in O(log N) via ZREVRANK.
ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 10 on a SQL players table has to re-sort the whole table on every query (unless very cleverly indexed, and even then it still can't return rank cheaply).
'Load everything then sort in the app' is wrong on both axes — complexity (dragging a million rows just to keep 10) and bandwidth (shipping a million records over the network every request).
That's why a real-time leaderboard for millions of players reaches for a sorted set instead of SQL or app-side sorting.
Three discrete GET/DECRBY/INCRBY commands race right between the read and the write.
Concretely: two clients both GET and see enough funds, both DECRBY, and the balance can go negative because one client's 'enough funds' decision has no idea the other client just subtracted.

Wrapping those three commands in MULTI/EXEC doesn't save you, because MULTI/EXEC only batches multiple commands to run in one shot — it does not let you read a value and then branch logic (if/else) on that value inside the transaction.
Checking 'enough funds or not' still has to happen by reading first on the client side before sending the write, and that exact gap is where the race happens.
Redis runs commands on a single execution thread.
A Lua script is executed as ONE uninterruptible command — from the GET of the source balance through DECRBY to INCRBY — so no client can interleave in the middle.
As a result the check is evaluated exactly at the moment of the write — the decision always uses the current balance, and the 'both see enough funds then both subtract' situation disappears entirely.
GEO keys in Redis are stored as sorted sets scored by a geohash value, so a radius search is a bounding-box scan over that sorted set rather than a separate dedicated spatial index.

`GEOSEARCH ... FROMLONLAT ... BYRADIUS` performs both the bounding-box scan and the distance filtering, including the haversine math, entirely on the server, so pulling every member back to the application and computing distance in a loop duplicates work Redis already does natively.

Fetching every member of a key with `ZRANGE key 0 -1` and then issuing one `GEOPOS` call per member turns a query that should be near-instant into O(n) network round-trips, and because Redis processes commands on a single thread, each extra round-trip adds queuing delay for every other client sharing that Redis instance.

A single key that holds every record regardless of region is both a big key, since it grows unbounded as more data is added, and a hot key, since every read request in the system touches that same key.
On Redis Cluster a key lives in exactly one hash slot, which pins an entire GEO key to a single shard — an oversized global GEO key can never be spread across nodes no matter how large it grows.

The fix for the Cluster and hot-key problem is to partition data into smaller keys scoped to a region or city, sized to a reasonable member count, re-bucketing points near a region boundary as needed so a search still hits only one key.

A thorough PR review separates must-fix correctness and performance issues, such as doing distance filtering in application code instead of in Redis or using an unpartitioned global key, from minor stylistic cleanups, and explains why each issue matters rather than only stating the fix.

Correctness of a server-side radius search can be verified by seeding a handful of known points with GEOADD, running the radius query, and asserting the result set is exactly the points within the given radius sorted by ascending distance, with no manual distance-calculation loop present anywhere in the handler or the test.
Reading an entire Redis list with `lrange(key, 0, -1)` is an O(N) operation — Redis has to walk and serialize every element in the collection, no matter how many entries the caller actually needs.
Because Redis executes commands on a single thread, one request that pulls hundreds of thousands of list entries blocks every other client hitting that same instance for as long as the read takes.

A list that is only ever `lpush`ed and never trimmed grows without bound, so months of unchecked writes turn a small key into a huge one, even though the UI likely only ever displays the newest handful of entries.

Calling `ltrim(key, 0, N - 1)` right after every `lpush` caps the list to the newest N entries; `LTRIM` only discards elements outside the kept range rather than rescanning the survivors, so the trim stays cheap regardless of how large the list had grown before it.

Serving reads with a bounded `lrange(key, 0, pageSize - 1)` — or an explicit start/stop for real pagination — instead of `lrange(key, 0, -1)` limits every read to a fixed-size slice no matter how large the underlying list becomes.

Because `lpush` always inserts new entries at index 0, both capping the list with `ltrim` and reading only a bounded prefix preserve newest-first ordering, so the newest activity remains at index 0 throughout.

The two costs in the unbounded feed compound each other: an O(N) read that stalls the single Redis thread on every request, and memory that grows forever because nothing ever removes the oldest activities — fixing only one side leaves the other problem in place.

The fix can be verified with a test that pushes far more than N activities and asserts `llen` never exceeds N afterward, plus an assertion that the read endpoint only ever issues a bounded-range command rather than a full `0, -1` range.

When an `ioredis` `Cluster` client is constructed without a `scaleReads` option, the default `scaleReads: 'master'` sends every command — reads and writes alike — to the master that owns the key's hash slot, so the replicas never receive any read traffic at all.

Setting `scaleReads: 'slave'` (or `'all'`) makes ioredis issue `READONLY` on replica connections and route read-only commands such as `GET` to a replica, spreading a read-heavy workload like `product:${id}` lookups across otherwise idle replicas instead of piling it all onto the masters.

Replication from a Redis master to its replicas is asynchronous, so a value read from a replica can lag the master by some amount of time; only reads that can tolerate that staleness should be routed to replicas, while any operation that must observe its own very-recent write needs to stay pinned to the master.

Redis replicas exist primarily for availability and failover — when a master fails, one of its replicas is promoted to take over that slot range — but a replica does not accept writes and does not own any hash slots of its own.

Adding more replicas to masters that are already saturated does nothing to relieve that saturation unless the read routing is also changed, because an idle replica stays idle for reads until the client is explicitly configured to send read commands there.
Growing a Redis Cluster's actual write and keyspace capacity requires adding more masters and resharding hash slots onto them, not increasing the number of replicas attached to the existing masters.

"Availability" (surviving a master failure through promotion) and "capacity" (how much read/write throughput the cluster can absorb) are two distinct properties of a Redis Cluster, so a plan that only adds replicas improves the former without touching the latter.

A read-routing change like this should be validated with an actual load-test measurement — comparing read throughput/latency with reads sent to replicas versus everything pinned to masters — and by confirming write throughput is unchanged and still bounded solely by the number of masters, rather than trusting a code review alone.
